title: Solo beginner, three months, a voiced party RPG demo. Here is what the AI tools did and did not do.
author: ahmet_makes_games
selftext:
I'm a beginner at game development and I work alone. Three months ago I started a party RPG in Godot in the Pillars of Eternity shape: three dwarfs, real-time with pause or turn-based, dialogue with open skill checks, a companion who keeps score. The free demo went up on itch today: a tavern, a forest valley.

Since this sub is about the tools, here is the honest split.

What the tools did: Claude Code wrote nearly all of the code with me directing it, and the same session kept the design docs, the tests (330 test scripts) and the build pipeline. ElevenLabs voiced 1,022 lines, each with a per-line direction so grief and banter don't get the same delivery. Tripo and Meshy made the character and prop models; Mixamo animated them; Grok painted the cover.

What they did not do: decide anything. The story, the characters, every line of dialogue, the rules, which SRD mechanics to port and how, what a dwarf-scale doorway is, which of twelve takes of a line was the right one. Three months of my evenings went into that part, and into playing it and writing down what was wrong.

What surprised me: the tools are fast at the first version and slow at the last ten percent. A weapon that sits in a hand correctly took measurement scripts and four camera angles per fix, not a prompt. And a workflow that writes tests and docs with every change is the only reason the project survived its own size.

Everything is disclosed on the itch page. Windows and Mac. I'd like to hear what people here do about the parts I found hardest: voice direction and animation.

[https://aedgamesdev.itch.io/chaos-awakens](https://aedgamesdev.itch.io/chaos-awakens)

comments.author: Opening_Wafer_6584
comments.body:
Hey, Alex here from the Tripo Studio US team. Really liked the distinction you made between tools being fast at the first version and slow at the last 10%. That feels especially true for game assets once they actually have to interact correctly with the rest of the game.

Since you used both Tripo and Meshy for the characters and props, I’m curious where the most time-consuming 3D cleanup ended up being for you. Was it mostly equipment/character fitting like the weapon example, or were there other recurring problems with the generated assets once they got into Godot?

Also congrats on getting the demo out after only three months.

replies.author: ahmet_makes_games
replies.body:
Thanks Alex. Honest answer: the meshes themselves were the easy part. The time went into everything that has to agree with a number.

For props (Meshy), two things came up every single time. The model arrives normalised into a 1 m box centred on the origin, so every prop needed its real height restored and its pivot moved to where the game needs it: the floor point, a hinge edge, a wall plate. That became a Blender script with a per-prop entry rather than a hand step. The other was small floating slivers the generation leaves around a mesh, which a script now drops by size plus “touches nothing”. And anything whose job depends on an exact dimension, a rail gauge, a doorway you walk through, I ended up authoring instead of generating.

For characters (Tripo) it was all about the rig, not the surface. Rigging through Mixamo and then binding to a shared clip skeleton quietly moved the joints: shoulders ended up 18 to 27 percent outboard of where the mesh wanted them, and finger joints sat a few centimetres outside the finger skin, so no fist could close on a weapon. The fix was measurement scripts that read where the joints belong off the skin weights and move them back, then re-solving every grip. That’s the “last ten percent” I meant: a weapon in a hand is accepted only from four camera angles in the running game, and three characters shipped for weeks holding their weapons 7 cm outside their fists before I built that check. One more Tripo-specific thing: the meshes are split at every UV seam, so any “is this point inside the body” test by ray parity misreads them; I had to switch to a winding-number test.

Also, I used base colour only and flat shading to match the Synty environments, which is probably why the surface side was painless. Thanks for the congrats.

replies.author: Opening_Wafer_6584
replies.body:
This is extremely helpful, especially the distinction that the meshes themselves were fine and the real production cost came from everything needing to agree with exact measurements.

The prop normalization/pivot issue and the rig-joint drift are both great examples of that “last 10%” problem. I also like that you solved them with measurement scripts instead of accepting them as recurring manual cleanup.

The four-camera weapon check is a really good sanity test too. Thanks for laying this out so clearly.

comments.author: isomorphix19
comments.body: The weapon in hand thing is so real, took me way longer than the actual combat logic. For the cover I'd still run Grok's output through Magnific, it cleans up those weird painted edges nicely at itch thumbnail size.

replies.author: ahmet_makes_games
replies.body:
Glad it’s not just me. The hands ended up with their own tooling: a script that measures where the handle sits against the finger joints, and a rule that no grip gets accepted without screenshots from four angles. The first pass of every fix looked fine from one side and was 5 cm off from the other. Combat logic was a week; hands were on and off for a month.

Thanks for the Magnific tip, I hadn’t thought about the thumbnail size specifically. The cover is a crop of a bigger piece and the edges do go soft where the vortex meets the figure. I’ll run it through and compare at the size itch actually shows it. Did you find it kept the painted look, or did it push things toward photo detail?
